A novel has hundreds of pages to tell a story. A song has about three minutes, and most of that is a chorus that
repeats. So a song cannot tell a story the way a book does. It picks **one moment**, **one voice** and a few
**details that say more than they state**, and lets the music do the rest of the work. This lesson is about
the words and the shape of the story. [Story Songs 2](story-music.qmd) is about what the music does under them.

::: {.callout-note}
## MYP4: Rock and the Pop Ballads
*Art allows us to express our feelings and communicate our philosophies and ways of life effectively.* A story song
is the clearest case: the listener has to feel what happened without being told how to feel. Criterion A: investigate
how one ballad tells its story. Criterion B: your own intention, written before you start, for the story you want to tell
and the feeling you want the listener to leave with.
:::

## 1. Who is telling it?

Every story song has a **narrator**, and the choice of narrator decides what we can know.

| Point of view | Sounds like | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **First person** (*I*, *me*) | "I waited at the door." | Close and confessional. We only know what the singer knows, and the singer may be wrong, or lying to themselves. |
| **Second person** (*you*) | "You pack the last box." | Talks to someone, or tells the listener what they are doing. Feels like a letter, an accusation, or a memory. |
| **Third person** (*she*, *he*, *they*) | "He sold the car in May." | A step back. The singer is a reporter or a friend telling someone else's story. Easier to build a whole life in a few lines. |
| **A character who is not the singer** | A king, a soldier, a child | The singer plays a part. We can hear more than the character understands. |

**Try it.** Take this one fact: *someone is leaving town tonight.* Write it three times, once in the first
person, once in the second, once in the third, one line each. Which one makes you care most? Which one leaves the most unsaid?

## 2. Character, setting, and the turn

A story needs three things, even a three-minute one:

- **A character** who wants something. It can be small (to be forgiven, to leave, to be seen).
- **A setting**: a place and a time that the listener can see. One or two details are enough.
- **A turn**: the moment something changes. A story without a turn is a description.

Where the turn lands is a choice. In many ballads it comes in the **bridge**, which is why the bridge is the part of the song
that sounds different: new chord, new register, often quieter. The last chorus then has the same words as the first and means
something else, because the listener now knows what happened.

## 3. Show, don't tell

Telling names the feeling. Showing gives the listener a detail and lets them feel it for themselves. Below, the
left side is **told** and the right side **shown**. These are the site's own example lines, not from any song.

| Told | Shown |
|---|---|
| I was lonely after you left. | Two cups on the shelf, and I only use one. |
| We had a lot of good times. | The photo-booth strip is still stuck to the fridge door. |
| He was a hard worker. | He left the house in the dark and came home in the dark. |
| I was scared to tell her. | I rehearsed it in the car, then drove past her street. |

Notice what the shown lines have in common: an **object**, an **action**, a **time**, a **place**. None of them has a
feeling word. Yet you know the feeling.

**Try it.** Take a feeling word (*proud, embarrassed, jealous, relieved*). Write one line that shows it with
an object and an action, and no feeling word. Swap with a partner. Can they name the feeling?

## 4. What each section is for

Pop form (see [Pop Forms](/theory/pop-forms.qmd)) is also a way of **pacing a story**.

| Section | Job in the story |
|---|---|
| **Verse 1** | Set the scene. Who, where, when. A concrete image. |
| **Pre-chorus** | Lean forward: the pressure builds and the question is asked. |
| **Chorus** | Say the feeling, or the idea, plainly. The same words each time. This is the part people remember. |
| **Verse 2** | Complicate it. Something happens, or we learn something that changes how we see verse 1. |
| **Bridge** | The turn. A new view, a new voice, or the moment it all comes to a head. |
| **Last chorus** | Same words, new meaning. Often one line is changed, or the band drops out so the line is heard by itself. |
| **Outro** | Leave a final image, or leave the question open. |

A common mistake is to tell the whole story in verse 1, and then have nothing left to say. Keep something back for verse 2 and the bridge.

## 5. Three shapes a story song can take

1. **One moment.** The whole song is a single scene seen from inside. Verse 2 is the same night, a bit later. Little plot, a lot of feeling.
2. **A journey through time.** Verse 1 is the past, verse 2 the present, the bridge or last verse the future (or the reverse).
3. **A letter or a conversation.** The song is spoken to someone. The story is what we work out from what is said, and what is not.

Most ballads you know are one of these. Decide which one before you write; it decides what each verse is for.

## 6. Story map: fill it in while you listen

Pick a ballad (the site's [Words & Chords](/songs/index.qmd) has some, or use your own) and listen to it
once for the story and once for the music. Fill in one row per section. Your answers are saved in this browser.

</div>

<script>
(function () {
  var KEY = 'story-map-v1', ROWS = ['Verse 1', 'Chorus', 'Verse 2', 'Chorus', 'Bridge', 'Last chorus'];
  var st = { title: '', pov: '', turn: '', rows: ROWS.map(function (n) { return { s: n, a: '', b: '', c: '' }; }) };
  try { var raw = localStorage.getItem(KEY); if (raw) st = JSON.parse(raw); } catch (e) {}
  function save() { try { localStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify(st)); } catch (e) {} }
  var body = document.getElementById('sm-body');
  function cell(r, k, tag) { var td = document.createElement('td'), f = document.createElement(tag); if (tag === 'input') f.type = 'text';
    f.value = r[k]; f.addEventListener('input', function () { r[k] = f.value; save(); }); td.appendChild(f); return td; }
  function draw() { body.innerHTML = ''; st.rows.forEach(function (r) { var tr = document.createElement('tr');
    tr.appendChild(cell(r, 's', 'input')); tr.appendChild(cell(r, 'a', 'textarea')); tr.appendChild(cell(r, 'b', 'textarea')); tr.appendChild(cell(r, 'c', 'textarea')); body.appendChild(tr); }); }
  var t = document.getElementById('sm-title'), p = document.getElementById('sm-pov'), u = document.getElementById('sm-turn');
  t.value = st.title || ''; p.value = st.pov || ''; u.value = st.turn || '';
  t.addEventListener('input', function () { st.title = t.value; save(); });
  p.addEventListener('change', function () { st.pov = p.value; save(); });
  u.addEventListener('input', function () { st.turn = u.value; save(); });
  document.getElementById('sm-add').addEventListener('click', function () { st.rows.push({ s: '', a: '', b: '', c: '' }); save(); draw(); });
  document.getElementById('sm-clear').addEventListener('click', function () { if (!confirm('Clear the whole map?')) return;
    st = { title: '', pov: '', turn: '', rows: ROWS.map(function (n) { return { s: n, a: '', b: '', c: '' }; }) }; save(); t.value = ''; p.value = ''; u.value = ''; draw(); });
  draw();
})();
</script>

## 7. Try it

- **Everyone:** write the same fact (*someone is leaving town tonight*) in three points of view (section 1). Choose one and say why.
- **Listeners:** fill in the story map for a ballad you chose. Where is the turn? What changes in the last chorus?
- **Writers:** go on to [Story Songs 5: Writing a Narrative Lyric](story-lyric.qmd).
- Next: [Story Songs 2: Music That Follows the Story](story-music.qmd).
